q: According to Bohr's second postulate, the angular momentum of an electron in an allowed orbit is
o: an integral multiple of h/(2 pi)
why: L = n h/(2 pi), quantization condition for allowed orbits.

q: The energy of the nth orbit of a hydrogen atom is given by
why: En = -13.6/n^2 eV, standard Bohr model result for hydrogen.

q: The spectral series of hydrogen corresponding to transitions ending at n = 1 is called the
why: Transitions ending at n=1 (ultraviolet region) form the Lyman series.

q: An electron transition from n=3 to n=2 in hydrogen releases energy equal to
why: E3 = -1.51 eV, E2 = -3.4 eV; released energy = (-1.51)-(-3.4) = 1.89 eV, a Balmer line.

q: The nuclear radius R depends on mass number A as
why: R = R0 A^(1/3), with R0 ≈ 1.2 fm, giving nearly constant nuclear density.

q: Nuclear density is approximately the same for all nuclei because
o: nuclear volume is independent of A
nuclear volume (R^3) is proportional to A
why: Since R proportional to A^(1/3), volume proportional to R^3 is proportional to A, keeping density nearly constant.

q: The binding energy per nucleon versus mass number A curve peaks (maximum stability) near
why: Iron-56 region has the maximum binding energy per nucleon (~8.8 MeV), the most stable nuclei.

q: Both nuclear fusion (light nuclei) and fission (heavy nuclei) release energy because they move
o: away from the binding energy peak
towards the binding energy peak near A=56
why: Both processes move nuclei towards the more stable middle region of the BE/A curve, releasing energy.

q: The radioactive decay law gives the number of undecayed nuclei at time t as
why: Solving -dN/dt = lambda N gives exponential decay N = N0 e^(-lambda t).
